cim: Hiding beyond the visible: How artificial intelligence is enhancing multispectral camouflage
cim_eredeti: Hiding beyond the visible: How artificial intelligence is enhancing multispectral camouflage
szoveg_eredeti:
Hiding beyond the visible: How artificial intelligence is enhancing multispectral camouflage lead image

If you had to hide from another person, you might throw on a ghillie suit and move on. But what if it wasn’t a person you were hiding from, but a camera detecting heat and radio waves?

Multispectral camouflage is used to conceal objects from sensors that detect parts of the electromagnetic spectrum beyond the visible light range. But its traditional design process is slow, relying heavily on intuition and trial-and-error. Using artificial intelligence (AI) can help uncover less intuitive yet more effective structures while balancing conflicting objectives. Wang et al. reviewed the benefits and challenges of these developments.

The authors studied several computational methods, including particle swarm optimization and convolutional neural networks. Overall, a common benefit of AI was the ability to simultaneously integrate visual camouflage, infrared low-emissivity, and radar absorption — though typically with trade-offs. Its designs could also match natural backgrounds more accurately than conventional approaches.

Moreover, AI was capable to designing effective, yet less complex profiles.

“Simple multilayer film stacks optimized by AI may outperform more complex metasurface designs,” said author Cunhai Wang. “AI-generated designs generally had near-identical simulation performance to human-designed structures, but with much thinner or lighter profiles.”

However, these methods were not without drawbacks. For example, the genetic algorithm — which optimizes for a solution by iterating on generations of candidate solution populations — was computationally expensive with slow convergence, while Bayesian optimization algorithms struggled with very high-dimensional or nonlinear problems.

Integrating AI’s approaches into the real world also remained a challenge.

“AI-designed structures may require nanoscale precision that current manufacturing cannot achieve,” Wang said. “Simulation models may not perfectly capture the real electromagnetic and thermal behavior, leading to discrepancies between predicted and actual performance.”

Ultimately, this research is highly useful toward military and civilian applications, including anti-drone protection and thermal control. Despite their current downsides, Wang noted these techniques could be dependable moving forward.

“A closed-loop workflow consisting of AI-assisted design, simulation, fabrication, measurement, and AI model retraining appears as a reliable approach to next-generation multispectral camouflage technologies,” Wang said.

Source: “Artificial intelligence-driven multispectral camouflage technologies,” by Cunhai Wang, Chunyun Cheng, Dong Guo, Hao Chen, Yong Li, and Jingchong Liu, Applied Physics Reviews (2026). The article can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0314716 .
